summary: This informational document summarizes operational implications of the IPv6 extension headers in RFC 8200 and analyzes why packets with them are often dropped on the public Internet.

plainLanguage.summary:
An IPv6 packet can carry a list of extra headers before the real protocol header. A router has to read the whole list to find out what is inside, and that is slow.

So many routers and firewalls simply discard such packets. This RFC sets out why, so that the problem can be fixed rather than worked around.

questions: why are ipv6 extension headers dropped
how do routers handle ipv6 packets with extension headers
why do firewalls filter ipv6 extension headers
what is an ipv6 extension header
subtitle: Why network devices often throw away IPv6 packets that carry extra headers.

tldr.problem: IPv6 lets a packet carry a chain of extra headers, and routers have to read the whole chain to find the transport protocol underneath. That is work that many routers were not built to do.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC explains the hardware limits of packet forwarding, the reasons a router needs to look at transport-layer information, and where different implementations parse the header chain differently.
tldr.outcome: The RFC does not recommend dropping these packets. It explains why they are dropped today, so that device support can improve and so that the issue is taken into account in standards work.

today: RFC 9098 is an Informational RFC and has not been obsoleted. It is an analysis rather than a recommendation: the RFC states that it does not recommend dropping packets with IPv6 extension headers, only that it documents why they are dropped today. The security considerations point back to Section 8.4, and the RFC introduces no new security issues of its own.

sections.title: Why Extension Headers Are a Problem in Practice
sections.content:
IPv6 extension headers allow the protocol to be extended, and they support core functions such as IPv6 fragmentation. Common limits in how devices are built make extension headers a challenge for routing equipment and middleboxes, and there is evidence that IPv6 packets carrying extension headers are deliberately dropped on the public Internet in some circumstances.

The RFC states three goals: to raise awareness of the operational and security implications of the extension headers in RFC 8200 and give reasons why some networks drop those packets; to point out where current device support for IPv6 is suboptimal, so that it can be improved; and to highlight operational issues so that standards work takes them into account.

The RFC is careful about what it is not. It analyses the operational challenges that extension headers create and documents some of the operational reasons why such packets are dropped on the public Internet. It is not a recommendation to drop them, but an analysis of why they are dropped now.
sections.plainLanguage:
Extension headers are part of the IPv6 design, but many routers struggle with them. The result is that packets with them often vanish.

The RFC explains the reasons, so that the problem gets fixed rather than hidden.

sections.title: How the IPv6 Packet Differs from IPv4
sections.content:
Comparing the two packet structures explains most of the trouble.

An IPv4 header has a variable length. The "Internet Header Length" field of the mandatory header gives the header size, which must be between 20 octets, the minimum, and 60 octets, leaving room for at most 40 octets of options. The upper-layer protocol type is given by the "Protocol" field in that same mandatory header.

IPv6 took a different approach. Instead of a variable-length header, the IPv6 packet looks like a linked list: a mandatory fixed-length header, then an arbitrary number of optional extension headers, with the upper-layer header last in the chain. Each extension header usually states its own length, unless the length is implied by its type, and states the "next header" type that follows it in the chain.

Three consequences follow. RFC 8200 requires the whole header chain to fit in the first fragment of a packet, which limits the chain to the size of the path maximum transmission unit. Apart from that limit there is no limit on how many extension headers a packet may carry, so there is no upper bound on how deep into the packet the upper-layer protocol header may sit. And the only way to find the upper-layer protocol type, or the upper-layer protocol header itself, is to parse the entire chain in sequence from the mandatory header onwards.
sections.plainLanguage:
IPv4 puts its options inside one header of known length, so a router can jump straight to the protocol. IPv6 uses a list of headers instead, so a router has to walk the list to find the protocol underneath.

Nothing limits how long that list can be, except the size of the packet on the path.

sections.title: What Earlier Work Already Said
sections.content:
Several earlier documents in the IETF had already touched on these issues. An operators' document gives the rationale for dropping IPv6 fragments. A draft on long header chains discusses the problems they cause. A parsing guideline describes how differences between implementations in reading extension headers can let traffic slip past security controls, and sets out a common way to parse them. A security analysis covers both the security implications of extension headers and the operational implications of dropping packets that carry them. RFC 7113 shows how some Router Advertisement Guard implementations can be evaded using extension headers, and RFC 8900 analyses the fragility that IP fragmentation introduces.

A number of RFCs have since addressed the topic and updated RFC 2460, an earlier version of the IPv6 standard, with the results folded into the current core standard and the node requirements. RFC 5095 deprecates Routing Header Type 0. RFC 5722 covers overlapping fragments. RFC 7045 clarifies how intermediate nodes should handle extension headers. RFC 7112 forbids fragmenting the header chain itself. RFC 6946 improves the handling of "atomic" fragments, and RFC 8021 deprecates generating them. RFC 8504 clarifies the processing rules and lets hosts limit how many options an extension header may carry, while RFC 7739 recommends how to generate fragment identification values that cannot be guessed, and RFC 6980 recommends against combining IPv6 fragmentation with Neighbor Discovery. RFC 8200 also relaxed the older rule that every node must examine the Hop-by-Hop Options header, so that only nodes configured to do so have to.

Several studies have measured how much of this traffic is dropped. Two give preliminary measurements of dropped packets with extension headers, RFC 7872 gives more comprehensive results and the method behind them, and two more measure drops caused by IPv6 fragmentation when talking to DNS servers.
sections.plainLanguage:
Most of the background is already known. Earlier documents looked at dropping fragments, at long header chains, and at the fact that different devices read the same packet differently.

This RFC does not repeat that work. It pulls it together and adds the operational picture.

sections.title: The Limits of Packet-Forwarding Hardware
sections.content:
Most carrier-grade routers use dedicated hardware, such as application-specific integrated circuits or network processing units, to decide how to forward packets across their internal fabrics. A common method is to send a small part of the arriving packet to a lookup engine with specialised hardware, such as ternary content-addressable memory or reduced latency dynamic random-access memory, to work out the next hop.

There is a trade-off here, because the amount of data sent to the lookup engine limits how fast that engine can work. Send more and the engine can look further into the packet, but the router's overall forwarding rate falls. Send less and the router is faster, but the engine may not be able to look far enough into the packet to decide what to do with it. The RFC notes that some contemporary high-end routers are known to inspect up to 192 bytes, while others are known to parse up to 384 bytes of header.

If the hardware cannot make a forwarding decision because the information it needs was not sent to the lookup engine, the router will normally drop the packet. Sending the packet to the control plane for deeper analysis was once common, but that is no longer feasible: the hardware forwarding capacity of a modern router is so much greater than the processing capacity of its control plane, and the link between the two is so much narrower than the forwarding plane could handle. Other platforms have a separate software forwarding plane, but its limited processor and its limited link produce the same throughput constraints. So if an IPv6 header chain is long enough to exceed the router's lookup capacity, the router may not be able to decide what to do with the packet and drops it.

Some forwarding engines manage the chain by recirculation, processing one extension header at a time and looping the packet back through the engine until no extension headers are left. This lets arbitrarily long chains be handled without the cost of a deep-inspection engine, but each packet then passes through the engine several times, which can reduce the data-plane throughput of the router depending on the configuration, the type of traffic and the capabilities of the hardware.
sections.plainLanguage:
Routers forward packets using specialised chips. Those chips can only look at so many bytes before deciding.

Send too much and the router gets slow. Send too little and the chip cannot see the information it needs, so the router throws the packet away.

sections.title: Why Devices Need Transport-Layer Information
sections.content:
Several kinds of intermediate system need information from the upper layers to make a forwarding decision.

Load sharing. With Equal Cost Multipath (ECMP), a device has to choose which interface to send a packet on. Round-robin use of the links is avoided because it reorders packets, so forwarding engines hash a tuple of fields taken from Layer 2 to Layer 4 and always send the same stream down the same path. That tuple usually includes the source and destination Media Access Control addresses, the source and destination IP addresses and, where possible, the transport ports. In IPv6 the flow label is expected to identify flows, so hash-based load sharing should not need the whole header chain. Support for the flow label is now widespread in host stacks, but its use for load balancing is still marginal, partly because of problems found in host implementations and middleboxes. If a device cannot derive a consistent tuple, data streams spread unequally across the links, which can lead to packet drops or reduced performance.

Infrastructure access control lists. These drop unwanted packets aimed at a network's own infrastructure, usually because direct external access to those addresses is unnecessary and can be used to attack router control planes. They typically need Layer 3 or Layer 4 criteria, for example permitting some ICMP echo traffic for troubleshooting and BGP sessions on an exchange point network while refusing other traffic from the same peer addresses. If a network cannot deploy them, the attack surface grows.

DDoS management. Layer 4 filtering for customers is applied as close to the edge as possible, often automated with BGP Flowspec. A website that normally handles only TCP ports 80 and 443 can be hit by a volumetric attack using NTP and DNS packets with randomised source addresses, which defeats source-based black-holing; blocking all UDP at the edge would solve it without hurting the web server.

Intrusion detection and prevention. These systems look for traffic patterns matching known attacks, inspecting application-layer traffic if they can and Layer 4 flows at the very least. Extension headers cause problems: they make the traffic more complex to process, an unknown extension header can stop the system from reaching Layer 4 information at all, and IPv6 fragmentation requires stateful reassembly, even for decoy traffic with forged source addresses. The result is that packets with extension headers are often dropped at the ingress of networks that deploy such systems.

Firewalling. Firewalls filter on Layer 3 and Layer 4 and often on application-layer flows, and meet the same three problems as intrusion detection systems. A common policy is default deny, where everything is blocked and only expected traffic is allowed. Packets with extension headers are therefore often dropped by firewalls, either because of the difficulty they cause or because they were never explicitly permitted.
sections.plainLanguage:
Five common jobs need to know what is inside a packet, not just where it is going: spreading load across links, protecting a router's own addresses, filtering a flood, watching for attacks and enforcing a firewall policy.

Finding that information means reading every extension header, which is exactly what slow devices cannot do.

sections.title: Operational and Security Implications
sections.content:
When a device cannot find the Layer 4 header, it has three choices: drop the packet, forward it anyway, or process it outside the normal forwarding path. Forwarding anyway usually lets traffic slip past security controls. Processing it outside the fast path usually opens the door to denial-of-service attacks. So devices often simply drop such packets.

The Hop-by-Hop Options header has been especially troublesome, because the packet is normally punted to the control plane, and many operators drop IPv6 packets that carry it. Traffic differentiation cannot be done by the control plane, because that would overload the link between the forwarding plane and the control plane.

Some devices also cannot filter finely. An operator who wants to drop packets carrying Routing Header Type 0 may only be able to filter on the Routing Header type in general, so the policy applied is coarser than intended: drop all packets with a Routing Header, rather than only those with Type 0.

The security implications of extension headers fall into four categories: evading security controls; denial of service caused by processing requirements; denial of service caused by implementation errors; and issues specific to the type of extension header.

Unlike IPv4, where the IHL field points straight at the upper-layer protocol, the IPv6 structure is flexible and complex, and finding the upper-layer information requires examining every extension header. Any filtering that needs upper-layer information, even just the protocol type, can be sidestepped by putting extension headers between the main header and the upper-layer header. RFC 7113 describes this for the RA-Guard case, and the same technique could be used against other firewalls and filtering mechanisms. Differences between implementations in how they parse the chain can also be used to evade controls.

Extension headers can also affect throughput. Without mitigations such as dropping or rate limiting, an attacker could send a lot of IPv6 traffic carrying extension headers to mount a denial-of-service attack. How much performance suffers depends on the implementation. In the simplest case a packet with a Hop-by-Hop Options header goes through the slow path and the router's processor; a router enforcing an access control list that depends on upper-layer information, such as the protocol type or the TCP destination port, may have to process the whole chain for the same reason. The same applies to firewalls and intrusion detection systems.

IPv6 implementations, like all software, mature with time and wide deployment. Although the protocol itself has existed for over 20 years, serious bugs in extension header processing are still being found, and because there is little operational reliance on these headers the code paths are rarely exercised. The Fragment Header, used for fragmenting and reassembling IPv6 packets, has also picked up problems that were already known from IPv4, ranging from denial-of-service attacks to information leaks.
sections.plainLanguage:
A router that cannot read past the extension headers has to choose: drop the packet, forward it unchecked, or handle it slowly. Forwarding unchecked lets an attacker slip past a firewall. Handling it slowly lets an attacker overload the router. So the packet is dropped.

The RFC also notes that this code is rarely used, so it is still full of bugs.
